title: The Necessary Inventory
premise: Tamsin Reyes, a piano tuner who reads a house's history through its radiators and pipes, has lived in her late grandmother's Brooklyn brownstone like a tenant rather than an heir, unable to claim it. When she finds a box of undelivered letters behind the wardrobe — written by her grandmother to a man named Elias Okonkwo, whose photograph sits unexplained on the mantel — she discovers the house was never fully hers: Elias holds half of it, and his family is coming to sell. As Tamsin traces the forty-year silence between two people who loved each other badly, she must decide whether justice means honoring a legal claim or a moral debt. In the end, she delivers the final letter herself to the dying Elias, and the two heirs choose to keep the house together — an inheritance remade as shared memory rather than contested property.
about_author: Astrid Villalobos is a former building superintendent in Crown Heights who spent a decade listening to the pipes of prewar houses before writing about them. Her fiction explores what families owe each other across silences, and this is her second novel.

chapters.title: The Tuner's Ear
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She tunes a piano in a dead woman's parlor, then returns to the brownstone she inherited but has never furnished, reading its radiators like braille. Establishes her estrangement from ownership and her gift for hearing what buildings remember. Emotional beat: loneliness disguised as competence.

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Moving the wardrobe to fix a cold radiator, she finds a shoebox of sealed, stamped, undelivered letters addressed to Elias Okonkwo, all in her grandmother Rosa's hand. The first letter mentions 'the money we took' and 'the room you built.' Emotional beat: vertigo — the house suddenly speaks a language she doesn't know.

chapters.title: The Stranger on the Mantel
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, with a letter excerpt. She matches the young man in the mantel photograph to the letters' author-addressee bond: Rosa and Elias were partners in something — a business, maybe more. A lawyer's old letter reveals Elias co-signed the deed in 1979. Emotional beat: inheritance curdling into question.

chapters.title: What the Radiators Said
chapters.summary: Elias's POV, 1979 flashbacks interleaved with Tamsin's present. Young Elias installs the boiler system himself; the chapters alternate his hope with Tamsin tracing his last known address. Emotional beat: falling in love with a stranger across time, and dreading what broke them.

chapters.title: The Money We Took
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Letters reveal Rosa used Elias's savings to cover a family emergency during the 1980 recession and never told him, letting him believe the business failed on its own. Tamsin finds the ledger confirming it. Emotional beat: shame inherited like furniture.

chapters.title: A Man Named Okonkwo Calls
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Elias's grandson Devon contacts Tamsin after finding her inquiry online; he wants to sell his grandfather's half immediately to pay medical debts. First tense meeting in the brownstone — two strangers circling the same grief. Emotional beat: hostility masking fear.

chapters.title: Forty Winters of Silence
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. The full rupture: Rosa's lie discovered, Elias's departure, the letters Rosa wrote every year and could never send. Tamsin reads them aloud alone in the cold house. Emotional beat: understanding without absolution — she sees both her grandmother's cowardice and her love.

chapters.title: The Eviction Notice
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Devon files to force the sale; a developer offers cash for the whole block. Tamsin faces losing the house either way unless she can reach Elias, now ninety-one and failing in a care facility upstate. Emotional beat: deadline pressure fusing legal stakes with moral ones.

chapters.title: The Last Undelivered Letter
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, climax. She drives to the facility and reads Rosa's final unsent letter — an apology written the week before her death — to Elias himself. He confesses he always knew about the money and stayed away out of pride, not ignorance. He signs over his half not to Tamsin but to 'the house's next keeper,' on one condition. Emotional beat: forgiveness arriving just inside the door of too late.

chapters.title: Bleeding the Radiators
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, resolution. Elias dies in spring; Devon, moved by the letters, withdraws the sale and instead moves into the ground floor while Tamsin keeps the upper rooms. Together they bleed the radiators, releasing trapped air until the whole house hums warm. Emotional beat: inheritance completed — not property transferred, but memory finally circulating.
